content:
In a debate on the Islamic dilemma, a Muslim scholar argued that the Quran may reread the Torah and the Gospel in its own light, as the New Testament rereads the Hebrew Bible. A Christian in the audience then granted, for the sake of argument, that the Quran is true, and asked a fair question. By the same reasoning, why should Muslims not reread the Quran in the light of Joseph Smith, or of Bahá'u'lláh? The speaker conceded it. He said the problem touches every religion with a scripture, and pointed to the Bahá'í faith as a live case.

The concession gave away more than it had to. The classical tradition has an answer, and the eight entries below set it out: what the Quran says about the last prophet, how the Prophet ﷺ explained it, how the Bahá'í and Ahmadi readings differ, and why rereading by a later revelation does not open an endless chain. Each entry says how strong it is, and the last one says plainly where the argument works only for someone who already accepts the Quran. The dilemma itself is answered in The Islamic Dilemma, and the Christian side of the same test is in The Christian twin of the Islamic dilemma. How one scripture rereads another, from Daniel to the Quran, is in How does scripture reread scripture?.

The verse is 33:40: مَّا كَانَ مُحَمَّدٌ أَبَآ أَحَدٍ مِّن رِّجَالِكُمْ وَلَـٰكِن رَّسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَخَاتَمَ ٱلنَّبِيِّـۧنَ, "Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but he is the Messenger of God and the seal of the prophets. And God has full knowledge of all things."[1] The verse came down after the Prophet ﷺ married Zaynab, the former wife of his adopted son Zayd, and it closes the question of whether Zayd was his son.

Al-Tabari (d. 310/923) glosses the phrase in one line: he is the one "who sealed prophethood and stamped it, so that it will not be opened for anyone after him until the Hour comes." He reports Qatada's gloss of "seal of the prophets" as "the last of them".[2]

Al-Tabari also records two readings of the word. Most readers of the garrison cities read khātim, "the one who sealed", and he notes that the codex of Ibn Mas'ud had "but a prophet who sealed the prophets". Al-Hasan and 'Asim read khātam, the reading of the Hafs text now printed in most copies, which he explains as "the last of the prophets", like the wine of 83:26 whose khitām, its end, is musk.[3] Both readings land in the same place. One names the act of sealing, the other the last in line.

Ibn Kathir (d. 774/1373) is blunter. "This verse is an explicit text that there is no prophet after him," he writes, "and if there is no prophet after him, then there is no messenger after him, all the more so," because every messenger is a prophet and the reverse does not hold.[4] The choice of al-nabiyyīn, the wider word, is the point. The difference between the two words is set out in Nabi and rasul. Strength: firm. No classical commentator read the verse as leaving the door open.

The plainest commentary on 33:40 comes from the man it names. Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: "My likeness and the likeness of the prophets before me is that of a man who built a house, made it fine and beautiful, except for the place of one brick in a corner. People walked around it, admired it, and said: why has this brick not been put in place? I am that brick, and I am the seal of the prophets."[5]

The picture is careful. The house was already fine. Ibn Hajar notes that each earlier prophet's law was complete for its own people, and the brick completes the building as a whole.[6] A finished house has no gap left for another brick.

Two other reports in al-Bukhari say it without a picture. "The Children of Israel were led by the prophets. Whenever a prophet died, another prophet succeeded him. And there is no prophet after me, and there will be caliphs." And when he left 'Ali in charge of Medina during the march to Tabuk: "Are you not content to stand to me as Aaron stood to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me?"[7] Ibn Kathir collects about a dozen reports of this kind under 33:40 and calls them mutawātir, reported by so many Companions that collusion is ruled out.[8]

The second report matters for this question. It names the pattern of Israel, prophet after prophet, and says the pattern stops with him. Leadership continues in the caliphs, who are not prophets. The same reports are discussed from another angle in Where did Jesus say he is God?. Strength: firm. The reports are in the two Sahih collections and need no further grading.

Two further verses close the gap a later prophet would need. In 5:3, revealed at 'Arafa during the Farewell Pilgrimage: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion."[9] In 15:9: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian."[10]

Ibn Kathir joins 5:3 to 33:40 himself. He calls the verse the greatest favour of God to this community, "since He completed their religion for them, so they need no religion other than it, and no prophet other than their prophet. For this reason God made him the seal of the prophets." On 15:9 he says God "is its guardian against change and alteration".[11]

Here the comparison in the debate breaks. The Muslim reading of the earlier books rests on two claims: that their wording passed through human hands, and that a later revelation may judge their meaning. A later claimant facing the Quran has neither to hand. The text is guarded by promise, and its meaning was fixed by the Prophet ﷺ in the reports of entry 2. How the transmission of the text was checked is in Preservation and truth. Strength: firm as a statement of what the Quran claims; whether the claim is true is the subject of entry 8.

The debate leaned on 5:48, where the Quran is "confirming that which preceded it of the Scripture and as a muhaymin over it."[12] Ibn Kathir glosses muhaymin as trustee, witness and judge over every book before it, and he gives the reason. God made this book "the last of the books and their seal, the most comprehensive, the greatest and the most precise of them," and then, in the same passage, he quotes 15:9: God took on its protection Himself.[13]

For the commentator, the book judges because it is the last, and it is the last because it is kept. A later book that claimed to judge the Quran would have to claim the same two things, and 33:40 has already said there will be no prophet to bring it.

One honest limit. The word muhaymin on its own does not say "once". That comes from 33:40 and 5:3, read together with 5:48, as Ibn Kathir reads them. What the Quran says about the Torah and the Gospel in full is in The Quran's verses on the Torah and the Gospel. Strength: moderate on the word alone, firm on the three verses together.

The speaker in the debate was right that the question is a real one. Two movements that grew up among Muslims in the nineteenth century accept 33:40 and read it differently.

The Bahá'í faith began in Iran with the Báb in 1844 and with Bahá'u'lláh (1817 to 1892). Bahá'ís accept the Quran as revelation and its text as intact. They read the seal as closing the cycle of prophecy that ran up to Muhammad, and hold that God continues to send what they call Manifestations of God, of whom Bahá'u'lláh is the latest for this age. In their reading, the seal ends one era and leaves revelation itself open.

The Ahmadiyya movement was founded in Qadian, in the Punjab, by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835 to 1908). The larger branch reads khātam as a seal in the sense of a stamp of approval: Muhammad is the most excellent of the prophets, no prophet brings a new law after him, and a prophet subordinate to him and within his community can still come. They hold that Mirza Ghulam Ahmad was that prophet. The smaller Lahore branch holds that he was a reformer (mujaddid) and makes no claim of prophethood for him.[14]

Both readings have to set aside the commentators of the first centuries, who read the verse as "the last of them", and the Prophet's own words in entry 2. The report of the Children of Israel is the hardest for the Ahmadi reading, since the prophets of Israel after Moses kept his law, which is the kind of prophet that reading allows, and the report says there will be none. Sunni and Shia scholars alike reject both readings. Strength: firm on the language and the early record. Both communities hold their readings in good faith, and this article answers their arguments and nothing else.

Joseph Smith (1805 to 1844) published the Book of Mormon in 1830 and taught that God speaks through living prophets with an open canon. The Book of Mormon makes the case for further scripture in so many words. It imagines readers who say, "A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible, and there cannot be any more Bible," and answers them, "Wherefore murmur ye, because that ye shall receive more of my word?"[15]

The Latter-day Saints make no claim about the Quran. Their quarrel is with closed Christian canons, and the questioner's case of Joseph Smith rereading the Quran is a hypothetical. It still tests the principle, so it gets the same answer as the Bahá'í case. A claimant who accepts the Quran inherits 33:40. A claimant who does not accept it is outside the question, which granted the Quran's truth at the start. Strength: firm as a reply to the question as asked.

The debate's principle, call it revelatory exegesis, says a true later revelation may reread an earlier one. The principle carries a condition: it works only when the later revelation is true, and that has to be shown on other grounds. The tradition gives four tests a later claim has to pass.

First, it must keep God one and wholly other. A claim that brings God into a creature, or a creature up to God, fails before anything else is weighed. This is the test of al-tawḥīd, and every prophet of the Quran passes it.

Second, it must take the earlier book at its word about what comes next. The Quran reads the Torah and the Gospel as pointing forward to a messenger: it speaks of the prophet "whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel," and has Jesus bring "good tidings of a messenger to come after me."[16] The Quran says the line ends (33:40, 5:3). A later claimant must overturn the plain sense of the book he claims to fulfil, while the Quran claims to complete books that, in its reading, expected more.

Third, its predictions must come true. The Torah gives the test: "When a prophet speaks in Yahweh's name, if the thing doesn't follow, nor happen, that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken."[17] Ibn Kathir adds the moral test under 33:40: the false claimants of Arabia were known by their lies and their conduct, while the prophets were known for truth and uprightness.[18]

Fourth, it must not need the earlier messenger to have misunderstood his own message. The Prophet ﷺ explained the seal in the reports of entry 2. A reading of 33:40 that he and his Companions did not hold asks Muslims to believe the man who received the verse got it wrong. Strength: moderate. Christians answer the second test with Hebrews 1:1 to 2, which says God "has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son," and with Jude 3, on "the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints."[19] So both sides claim finality. The tests decide between them only together with the case for each book.

A fair answer says how far it reaches. Three grades apply here.

Firm: inside the question as it was asked. The Christian questioner granted that the Quran is true. On that ground, 33:40, 5:3, the reports of entry 2 and the commentators settle it: a true Quran rules out a later prophet, so no later prophet may reread it. The concession in the debate was unnecessary.

Moderate: on historical ground. Anyone can check that the earliest Muslim readers took the seal to mean the last, and that the Bahá'í and Ahmadi readings came twelve centuries later. That shows what the verse meant to its first hearers. It does not show that the verse is from God.

Internal to faith: the claim that God closed prophecy with Muhammad ﷺ stands or falls with the claim that the Quran is from God. A reader who doubts that will not be moved by 33:40, and he should not be. The case for the Quran rests on other ground: its text, its transmission and the life of the man who brought it, set out in Who wrote the Quran?. Strength: internal to faith. The argument closes the door to a later prophet for Muslims, and leaves every reader free to test the Quran itself.

The bottom line

The audience question was a good one, and it has an answer. The Quran names its messenger the seal of the prophets, the earliest commentators read that as the last, the Prophet ﷺ said there is no prophet after him, and the Quran calls the religion complete and its text guarded. Rereading by a later revelation is a conditional principle, and the Quran itself removes the condition for anyone who accepts it. For anyone who does not, the question moves back to whether the Quran is from God. Allāhu aʿlam.
